content: Rifampin, isoniazid, and pyrazinamide are indicated for use during the initial phase of short-course treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis, typically lasting two months. The dosing regimen is weight-based: patients weighing less than 44 kg should take 4 tablets orally once daily, those weighing 44–54 kg should take 5 tablets orally once daily, and those weighing more than 55 kg should take 6 tablets orally once daily. Following the initial phase, treatment with rifampin and isoniazid should continue for at least four months. Prolonged treatment may be necessary if the patient remains sputum or culture-positive, if resistant organisms are present, or if the patient is HIV-positive. Safety and efficacy in patients under 15 years of age have not been established. Rifampin significantly decreases the plasma levels or therapeutic effects of several drugs by inducing hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. This interaction often results in reduced efficacy of the co-administered drug and may lead to therapeutic failure or resistance development. Co-administration of rifampin with the following drugs is contraindicated due to these effects: 1. Artemether/lumefantrine: Rifampin reduces serum concentrations, leading to loss of antimalarial efficacy. 2. Atazanavir: Rifampin increases metabolism, resulting in reduced antiviral efficacy and potential viral resistance. 3. Bictegravir: Rifampin decreases plasma concentrations, leading to loss of therapeutic effect and resistance development. 4. Cabotegravir: Rifampin increases metabolism, reducing systemic exposure and virologic response. 5. Cariprazine: Rifampin affects the formation and elimination of active metabolites, with unclear net effects. 6. Cobicistat: Rifampin reduces therapeutic effects and may lead to resistance. 7. Cobimetinib: Rifampin decreases systemic exposure by over 80%, reducing efficacy. 8. Darunavir: Rifampin increases metabolism, leading to loss of antiviral efficacy and resistance. 9. Doravirine: Rifampin reduces plasma concentrations, leading to virologic failure and resistance. 10. Elbasvir/grazoprevir: Rifampin reduces therapeutic effects, making co-administration contraindicated. 11. Elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir DF: Rifampin reduces levels, leading to virologic failure and resistance. 12. Etravirine: Rifampin increases metabolism, reducing efficacy. 13. Fosamprenavir: Rifampin increases metabolism, leading to loss of antiviral efficacy and resistance. 14. Fostemsavir: Rifampin significantly decreases plasma concentrations of the active moiety, leading to virologic failure. 15. Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir: Rifampin significantly reduces plasma concentrations and therapeutic effects. 16. Irinotecan: Rifampin affects CYP2B6 metabolism, reducing efficacy. 17. Isavuconazonium sulfate: Rifampin reduces levels, making co-administration contraindicated. 18. Ledipasvir/sofosbuvir: Rifampin reduces sofosbuvir levels and active metabolite conversion, decreasing efficacy. 19. Lenacapavir: Rifampin reduces levels, making co-administration contraindicated. 20. Lomafarnib: Rifampin reduces levels, contraindicating co-administration. 21. Lorlatinib: Rifampin reduces levels; strong CYP3A inducers must be discontinued before initiating lorlatinib. 22. Lumacaftor/ivacaftor: Rifampin reduces ivacaftor exposure by 57%, decreasing efficacy. 23. Lurasidone: Rifampin reduces levels, contraindicating co-administration. 24. Mavacamten: Rifampin reduces levels via CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 metabolism. 25. Naloxegol: Rifampin reduces levels, making co-administration not recommended. 26. Nelfinavir: Rifampin reduces plasma concentrations, leading to therapeutic failure and resistance. 27. Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir: Rifampin reduces plasma concentrations, leading to virologic failure and resistance. 28. Ombitasvir/paritaprevir/ritonavir & dasabuvir: Rifampin reduces levels, decreasing efficacy. 29. Panobinostat: Rifampin reduces levels by ~70%, leading to treatment failure. 30. Pirfenidone: Rifampin reduces levels; strong CYP1A2 inducers should be avoided. 31. Praziquantel: Rifampin reduces levels, contraindicating co-administration. 32. Regorafenib: Rifampin reduces levels and increases exposure to active metabolites. 33. Rilpivirine: Rifampin reduces levels, leading to virologic failure and resistance. 34. Roflumilast: Rifampin reduces systemic exposure, decreasing therapeutic effectiveness. 35. Tipranavir: Rifampin reduces levels, leading to loss of antiviral efficacy and resistance. 36. Vandetanib: Rifampin reduces exposure by up to 40%, contraindicating co-administration. 37. Velpatasvir: Rifampin reduces levels, contraindicating co-administration. 38. Voriconazole: Rifampin increases metabolism, reducing efficacy. For certain drugs, rifampin co-administration is not recommended, and alternative therapies should be considered. These include: 1. Abemaciclib: Rifampin reduces plasma concentrations; alternative drugs should be used. 2. Abrocitinib: Rifampin reduces combined exposure, leading to reduced clinical response. 3. Acalabrutinib: Rifampin reduces levels; dose adjustments may be required if co-administration is unavoidable. 4. Adagrasib: Rifampin reduces levels; alternative drugs should be used. 5. Afatinib: Rifampin reduces levels; dose adjustments may be required. 6. Almotriptan: Rifampin reduces levels; alternative drugs should be used. 7. Alpelisib: Rifampin reduces levels; co-administration should be avoided. 8. Alprazolam: Rifampin reduces levels; alternative drugs should be used. 9. Amiodarone: Rifampin reduces levels; alternative drugs should be used. 10. Apixaban: Rifampin reduces exposure; alternative drugs should be used. 11. Apremilast: Rifampin reduces systemic exposure, leading to loss of efficacy. 12. Aprepitant: Rifampin reduces levels; alternative drugs should be used. 13. Aripiprazole: Rifampin reduces levels; alternative drugs should be used. 14. Atorvastatin: Rifampin reduces levels and increases toxicity risk; alternative drugs should be used. 15. Avapritinib: Rifampin reduces levels; alternative drugs should be used. 16. Axitinib: Rifampin reduces levels; alternative drugs should be used. In summary, rifampin's potent induction of CYP3A4 and other metabolic pathways significantly impacts the pharmacokinetics of numerous drugs, often necessitating avoidance or substitution to maintain therapeutic efficacy and prevent resistance.
